messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 69
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Financial Analyst
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 74

He is sixty-nine now, a widowed man who still introduces himself, almost automatically, as a financial analyst. Numbers have always given him a sense of order. For most of his adult life, he works in spreadsheets, forecasts, and quarterly reports, and at home he builds a quieter life with his wife, who teases him about balancing the checkbook to the penny. They are not dramatic people. Their routines are steady, ordinary, and deeply shared: coffee before work, dinner at the same corner of the table, small conversations carried across decades.

The event that divides his life into before and after happens three years ago. His wife is struck by a driver while crossing a street near their neighborhood grocery store. He is not with her when it happens. The first thing he remembers is the phone ringing and not recognizing the number. Then a stranger’s voice, controlled and practical, telling him there has been an accident and he needs to come to the hospital. He still describes the drive there in fragments: red lights that seem offensive, the feel of the steering wheel slipping in his hands, the irrational thought that if he parks close enough to the entrance, she will be all right.

At the hospital he sees blood on a sheet before he fully sees her. He remembers the machinery, the fluorescent light, a physician speaking in phrases he cannot hold onto. He keeps trying to ask the right question, as if precision might change the outcome. He has spent a career believing that if one examines the data carefully enough, one can reduce uncertainty. Instead he watches his wife die from injuries he cannot organize, predict, or repair.

In the weeks afterward, he moves like a man performing tasks written for someone else. He handles the paperwork, calls relatives, answers emails from colleagues, thanks neighbors for casseroles he does not taste. People tell him he is coping well because he remains composed. He returns to work quickly, thinking structure will help. He sits at his desk reviewing market summaries, but the numbers blur. He catches himself staring at columns on a screen without understanding what they mean. Sudden sounds—a dropped binder, a phone ringing sharply—send a jolt through him so intense he feels embarrassed, then angry. He begins staying late at the office, partly to avoid the silence at home and partly because he can no longer finish in eight hours what used to take four.

Nights become the worst part of the day. When he closes his eyes, his mind supplies images he never actually witnessed: his wife lying alone on the pavement, frightened, calling for him. Sometimes the hospital scene returns instead, especially the sheet, the lights, the helpless waiting. He wakes drenched in sweat, heart hammering, unsure for a moment what year it is. He starts sleeping in the den with the television on low because darkness and quiet make the images stronger. He tells himself this is temporary, just grief, just time doing what it does.

But time passes, and his world gets smaller rather than larger. He avoids the grocery store where she was headed that day. He drives several blocks out of his way to avoid the intersection. If he accidentally approaches it, his chest tightens and his hands go cold on the wheel. Once, stopped at a nearby light, he sees a woman in a coat similar to his wife’s and has to pull over to vomit. After that, he plans routes meticulously, checking maps the way he used to check financial statements, trying to prevent surprise.

He also avoids other people’s concern. Friends invite him to dinner, but he declines. He knows they mean well, yet ordinary conversation feels impossible. He cannot tolerate being told she would want him to move on. At work, younger colleagues notice he has become curt and impatient. If someone asks a vague question, he snaps. He hates this version of himself. He was once known for being steady, even generous with junior staff. Now he feels constantly on guard, as though catastrophe is not a past event but something stalking just outside the frame.

There is guilt threaded through nearly everything. He thinks he should have gone with her that afternoon. He should have insisted she let him drive. He replays small decisions with obsessive logic, searching for the moment the trajectory could have changed. He knows, in the abstract, that this kind of accounting is impossible, but he cannot stop performing it. It is the only way he knows to stay connected to her and to the day he lost her.

In the present, his apartment remains carefully maintained, almost museum-like. Her coat is still in the hallway closet. Some mornings he speaks to her photograph before leaving for work. He continues to function, to produce reports, to attend meetings, to pay bills on time. From the outside, he appears disciplined and intact. Inside, he feels split between the man who can still analyze risk for a living and the husband who learned, in one phone call, that the worst thing can happen without warning and never really end.
